howto.name: Paste the token
howto.text: Paste a JSON Web Token: three base64url parts separated by dots, header.payload.signature.

howto.name: Read the header and claims
howto.text: The header and payload are decoded to readable JSON, and time claims such as exp and iat are shown as dates, with a clear indication when the token has expired.

howto.name: Copy what you need
howto.text: Copy the decoded parts for a bug report or a test. The decoding happens on this page; the token is not uploaded to PrivaTools.

faq.q: Does this verify the token's signature?
faq.a: No, and that matters. The tool decodes and displays the contents; it does not check the signature against a key. A token that decodes cleanly may still be forged or tampered with, so never treat a decoded token as trusted.

faq.q: Why can anyone read my token's payload?
faq.a: Because a standard signed JWT is encoded, not encrypted. Base64url is reversible by anyone, which is why a JWT should never carry secrets such as passwords.
No. Decoding runs in JavaScript on this page and the token is not uploaded to PrivaTools. Even so, treat a live production token like a password and avoid pasting it into places you do not control.

faq.q: It says the token needs three parts.
faq.a: A signed JWT is three sections separated by two dots. A missing section usually means the token was truncated when copied, or it includes a prefix such as Bearer that should be removed.

faq.q: How do I read exp and iat?
faq.a: They are Unix timestamps in seconds: iat is when the token was issued and exp when it expires. The tool converts them to dates and highlights an expired token.
No. An encrypted token (JWE) has five parts and cannot be read without the key. This tool handles the common signed format.
